pi.name: E. Josie Clowney
pi.title: Associate Professor of Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology
pi.bio: E. Josie Clowney is a University of Michigan alumna from Grand Rapids, Michigan. She earned her PhD studying olfactory receptor choice with Stavros Lomvardas at UCSF and completed postdoctoral work on neural circuits for mate choice with Vanessa Ruta at Rockefeller University. She founded her lab in the Department of Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology at the University of Michigan in 2017 and was promoted to Associate Professor with tenure in 2024. Her awards include fellowships from the Sloan, Pew, Rita Allen, and McKnight Foundations.

description: The Clowney Lab investigates how neural circuits that drive survival behaviors (feeding, fighting, fleeing, mating, parenting, and sleeping) are organized in the brain and how that organization is produced during development. Using developmental biology, connectomics, imaging, genetics, and behavioral analysis, the lab studies the DNA-encoded recipes that build neurons and wire them into functional circuits, focusing on chemosensory circuits in the fruit fly. Projects examine how the male-specific transcription factor Fruitless generates sex-differentiated mating circuits, how randomized wiring in the mushroom body supports general-purpose learning, and how perturbing circuit development changes sensory coding and behavior. The lab also studies vertebrate genome organization, including how AT and GC sequence content relate to gene spacing and the evolution of neurodevelopmental genes.

areas.title: Sex-specific mating circuits
areas.summary: Examines how male fruit flies instinctively identify mates and initiate courtship, focusing on how the male-specific transcription factor Fruitless generates sex-differentiated neural circuits through molecular dissection, imaging, genetics, circuit mapping, and behavior.

areas.title: Randomized wiring in the mushroom body
areas.summary: Investigates general-purpose learning circuits that process evolutionarily unpredicted sensory information, using connectomics, developmental imaging, and transcriptional approaches to test whether a simple developmental algorithm generates learning capacity through non-deterministic patterning.

areas.title: Engineering development for olfactory coding
areas.summary: Tests theoretical predictions about circuit function by experimentally perturbing neural circuit development during embryogenesis and measuring the resulting changes in sensory coding and behavior.

areas.title: Vertebrate genome organization and transcriptional regulation
areas.summary: Analyzes how chromosomal gene organization relates to regulatory control, examining how AT/GC sequence content correlates with genomic spacing and gene evolution in humans.
